extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy (Aristotle)
extracted.subtask_description: A classical framework for assessing moral character and social behaviors (liberality, magnificence, great-mindedness, anger, truthfulness, jocularity, etc.) as set out in Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics. Emphasises the mean between excess and defect, with examples and anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberality vs Stinginess
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberality concerns appropriate giving and receiving of wealth; Stinginess is receiving from improper sources or in improper amounts and submitting to disgrace for the sake of gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stinginess is characterised by 'base-gaining' and accepting small, improper gains (examples: usurers lending small sums at large interest, brothel-keepers), and is the contrary of liberality. Distinguish between wicked (those who plunder great things) and stingy (those who stoop to small, disgraceful gains).

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence (fitting expense on a large scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: A virtue like liberality but limited to large-scale, expensive expenditures — 'fitting expense on a large scale'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The magnificent person spends largely and in good taste, aiming at beauty and fitness of the work rather than minimal cost. Expenditures must be proportionate to the work and to the doer (rank and means). Appropriate objects include public, honourable expenses (temple offerings, public spectacles, equipping triremes, furnishing a house befitting one's wealth, long-duration works). A poor man attempting magnificence is foolish (out of proportion). The motive is honour; spending should be done with pleasure and without mean precision in calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulgar Profusion (excess of magnificence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive, improper spending intended to display wealth rather than to serve honourable ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterised by showing off, spending lavishly on trivial or improper objects and in improper manner (example: giving actors purple in the first scene to create spectacle). The vulgar profuse person spends much where little is needed and little where much is needed, aiming at admiration rather than fittingness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meanness (defect of magnificence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deficiency in expenditure on large or honourable objects; contrives to spend the least and spoils effects by skimping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mean (deficient) man is procrastinating and laments expense. Even where he spends most, he omits some trifle that spoils the whole effect. Both meanness and vulgar profusion are faulty because they fail to be fitting, though not necessarily disgraceful in social terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great-mindedness (megalopsychia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuing oneself highly and justly; greatness with propriety, having honour as the chief object-matter and acting accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The great-minded man estimates himself at his real worth, especially regarding honour, and so bears himself rightly in honour and dishonour. He should be genuinely good (virtue is necessary). Traits include moderation towards wealth and power, disdain for trivial honours, willingness to incur great risks for worthy ends, reluctance to ask favours but readiness to do services, loftiness towards the very great and affability to middling persons, reserve and preference for reality over appearance, slow deliberate speech and bearing. Must avoid arrogance and superficial imitation of greatness (vanity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-mindedness and Vanity (defect and excess relative to great-mindedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Small-mindedness: underestimating one's deserts; Vanity: overestimating oneself without grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small-mindedness causes one to shun honourable actions and external goods due to self-ignorance; Vanity leads to foolish attempts at honour and ostentation (dress, talk). Small-mindedness is more common and worse than vanity; both are contrasted to true great-mindedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper relation to Honour (mean between extremes)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a mean state in the pursuit and valuation of honour distinct from great-mindedness, appropriate for moderate and small matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may love honour rightly (praiseworthy) or in excess (ambition/love of honour from wrong sources) or be deficient (not desiring honour even when deserved). The mean exists though sometimes unnamed; specific judgment depends on particulars and moral sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meekness (mean with respect to Anger)
rubrics_metrics.description: Being angry at the right things, with the right people, in the right manner, at the right time, and for the right duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meekness (the praised mean) implies imperturbability and anger governed by reason. Excesses include passionateness (quick to anger but cools), choleric (constantly vehement), bitter-tempered (long-held resentment), and cross-grained (angry at wrong objects and vindictive). Defect (angerlessness) is also blameworthy when it prevents appropriate resentment and defence. Determination of right degree relies on particulars and moral sense; slight deviations may be excused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Intercourse Mean (between Over-Complaisant and Contentious)
rubrics_metrics.description: A balanced manner in social exchange: neither always acceding to give pleasure nor opposing for opposition's sake, but acting according to propriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mean is akin to an amiable, properly restrained friend: letting pass what should be let pass and objecting when proper. The Over-Complaisant always agrees to avoid causing pain; the Cross/Contentious opposes regardless of pain. The mean weighs what is noble and expedient, differentiates by rank and knowledge of persons, and may inflict small pains for greater consequent pleasure when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness (mean between Exaggeration and Reserve)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plain, matter-of-fact honesty about one's claims in life and speech: admitting what belongs to one neither more nor less than truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggerators claim more credit than due (worst), Reserved persons downplay or deny their real qualities (may appear refined). Braggarts exaggerate for glory; liars may lie for pleasure or gain. Truthfulness in indifferent matters marks a praiseworthy moral state and tends to promote truthfulness in weightier matters too.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jocularity / Tact in Jesting
rubrics_metrics.description: Jocularity as a mean between Buffoonery (excess) and Clownishness (defect): saying and hearing what is fit for a gentleman without causing pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The man of tact ('easy pleasantry') says and listens to jests appropriate to his station and audience, avoiding obscene or painful jests. He aims at refined, fitting humour (innuendo vs coarse obscenity). Buffoons pursue laughter at any cost, sparing neither self nor others; Clownish persons refuse to engage in jocularity and are sour. The refined jester is 'a law to himself'—self-restrained. Consider audience, education, and differing tolerances; some jocularity is indispensable as pause and amusement in life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shame as a feeling (not a moral virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shame is defined as 'a kind of fear of disgrace' and is treated as a feeling similar to fear rather than a stable moral state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shame produces physical effects (blushing) and is regarded as appropriate mainly to youth as a check on passion-driven wrongdoings. It differs from virtues which are stable dispositions governing action.
